title: How Ofqual are Killing English
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that Ofqual, the UK exams regulator, has failed in its core mission to maintain reliable English qualification standards, despite crediting the broader Gove-era reforms with genuinely raising standards after Tony Blair-era grade inflation and a corresponding fall in England's PISA rankings. His central evidence is the National Reference Test, a safeguard designed in 2013 to keep Ofqual honest by sampling Year 11 attainment in maths and English without exposing results to schools or students, and using them only to calibrate grade boundaries. Since 2017, Salles reports, the test has repeatedly shown weaker attainment at the crucial grade 4/5 English borderline, yet Ofqual has declined to act on the finding, even as evidence-based, retrieval-focused teaching has visibly improved elsewhere. He locates the cause specifically in the 2017 English specification's writing requirements, which he argues reward superficial technique, overloaded description, arbitrary single-word sentences, excessive punctuation, over genuine written communication, while England's reading performance on PISA has meanwhile improved. The piece closes with Salles positioning himself as filling the gap Ofqual has left, through training for English teachers.
points: Salles credits Michael Gove's reforms (ending modular exams, tasking Ofqual with halting grade inflation, benchmarking against Singapore/Hong Kong/Finland) with genuinely raising standards, despite his personal dislike of Gove.

The National Reference Test was designed as a safeguard against grade inflation by testing a hidden sample of Year 11s and using results only to calibrate grade boundaries, never as an accountability measure.

Since 2017, the test has repeatedly shown weakening English attainment at the 4/5 grade borderline, but Ofqual has declined to lower grade boundaries in response, which Salles calls a direct failure of the regulator's duties.
He attributes the decline specifically to the 2017 exam specification's writing requirements, arguing they reward 'turgid tricks' rather than genuine writing ability.
Salles contrasts this with reading, where England's PISA performance has improved, to argue the decline is isolated to writing instruction driven by a spurious curriculum.
quotes: Gove told us he had had enough of experts, and called teachers, academics and their unions who opposed him "the Blob". He pushed forward the Labour intitiative of academisation which may or may not have improved schools.
Between 2000 and 2009, England dropped down the rankings table from 7th to 25th for reading, 8th to 27th in maths, and 4th to 16th in science.

It was a simple and brilliant idea - The National Reference Test. A sample of each year 11 would sit a one hour paper in each of maths and English. The results would be kept from students and schools, so they would never be misused as accountability measures.

For the past couple of years, the test has detected that attainment around the 4/5 borderline in English language is weaker than when the test was first administered in 2017. If the process worked as intended, this would have led Ofqual to require grade boundaries to be changed so that fewer pupils achieved a grade 9-4 in English language.

Over that same period, teachers have become more focused on evidence, on research, on retrieval - their teaching has clearly improved. This is also borne out by the rise in the number of schools Ofsted has declared not to be failing.

To our shame, English teams overwhelmingly practise these ridiculous forms of writing - description overloaded with adverbs and adjectives, spurious colours, redundant vocabulary, arbitrary single word sentences and single sentence paragraphs.
Writing has become a ludicrous ticklist of turgid tricks to cross off in the exam paper, and in the curriculum.
